title: AI Coding Assistants Are Moving to Token Billing. Retries Now Cost Money
excerpt: Metered billing makes AI coding costs visible, but it also charges you for failed attempts and bloated context — which is where small teams actually lose money.
content:
Between March and September 2026, three of the four major coding assistants replaced flat subscriptions with metered billing. GitHub Copilot moved business seats to a request-based model, Cursor introduced usage tiers, and Anthropic's Claude Code shifted heavy users to per-token pricing. The stated reason was capacity: agents now run for minutes at a time, not seconds.

For a two-person team shipping a side product, the change is not neutral. It moves cost from a predictable line item to a variable that scales with how you work, not what you build.

Predictable cost, punishing retries

Metered billing makes the unit price visible. That is the advertised benefit, and it is real: you can forecast spend from token volume the way you forecast cloud spend. NIST's AI risk guidance makes the same point about measurement — you cannot manage what you do not meter.

The problem is what gets metered. An agent that fails twice and succeeds on the third attempt bills for all three. A flat subscription absorbed that; a token meter does not. Debugging a flaky prompt becomes a paid activity, and the incentive quietly shifts toward accepting the first plausible answer.

  • Flat seat: retries are free, quality work is encouraged
  • Token meter: retries are billed, users learn to stop early

The real cost driver is context, not generation

Teams that instrument their own usage keep finding the same shape. Output tokens are a small share of the bill; the bulk sits in what gets re-sent on every turn. A 40-page repository summary pasted into a system prompt is charged again with each message.

Anthropic's own pricing documentation separates input and output rates precisely because input dominates. OpenAI's API pricing page shows the same asymmetry, with cached input priced lower to discourage repeated full-context calls.

So the team that trims its context before switching vendors saves more than the team that shops for a cheaper per-token rate. The first intervention is cheaper and it compounds.

Hybrid pricing is the likely landing point

Pure metering is hard to sell to small teams because the variance is unbounded. Pure seats are hard to sustain because a single agent session can consume more compute than a month of autocomplete. The compromise already exists in cloud billing: a committed base with overage.

Expect seat-plus-allowance to become standard within two quarters. It gives buyers a ceiling and gives vendors a floor, and both sides have learned that fully variable pricing makes budgeting impossible for anyone under fifty people.

Where I land

Small teams should fix context handling before they renegotiate tooling. Measured against a token bill, a shorter prompt, a tighter retrieval set and a cached system message are the only levers that reliably cut spend without cutting output quality. Switching vendors first is a way to feel productive while the underlying waste stays in place.

The counter-argument is fair: if your usage is genuinely light, the cheapest vendor wins and engineering time is better spent on the product. That holds until the first long agent run, at which point the invoice becomes an engineering problem anyway.

FAQ

Does metered billing make small teams pay more than before?

Not automatically. Teams with steady, low-volume usage usually pay less. Teams that run long agent sessions pay more, because those sessions were previously subsidised by flat pricing.

What is the quickest way to cut a token bill?

Cut the context that gets re-sent every turn: trim system prompts, retrieve fewer documents, and cache stable instructions. Those changes affect every request, while switching models affects only the rate.

Will prices come down?

Per-token rates have fallen steadily, but the composition of usage has shifted toward longer contexts that consume more tokens per task, so bills have not fallen at the same pace.
